rubric.note: This is a high-quality output that clears the bar on the three double-weighted dimensions. R1 is exemplary — the constraint-first narrative is precise, arithmetically grounded, and avoids every generic opener trap. R2 is strong — sequencing is argued not assumed, with deadline windows, capacity logic, and goal-type ordering all present. R5 is good but not a 5: the agent recommends the planted trap (syn-another-big-bid) but partially mitigates it through the concentration flag and rebalance action — a senior consultant would have been more explicit about the tension between recommending a large restricted bid and the stated goal of multi-year unrestricted income. The fact/judgment architecture (R4) is the strongest structural feature of the output and sets a high standard. The main weaknesses are (a) the implicit validation of the volume-first instinct in the syn-another-big-bid recommendation, (b) the ordering of the recommendation list (strategic priority vs action urgency is slightly confused), and (c) the load weight of the JSON scaffolding which, while disciplined, is not fully invisible to the end user.

rubric.note: A high-quality output overall. The double-weighted dimensions (R6, R4, R2) are all excellent — R4 and R6 are genuine 5s. The kind-challenge handling of the Transforming Futures question is exactly what the case guidance asks for: facts cited, view stated, decision left with the user, enthusiasm respected. R2 sequencing is concrete and operationalised. The main deductions are: R1 slightly misorders the binding constraint for the specific question asked (the 20 July deadline is more immediately binding than the general concentration point); R7 has minor length/overlap issues; R5 misses one practitioner nuance about the cost-effectiveness of the small grant. No material errors of fact or sector-tone-deafness.

This is a high-quality output that satisfies virtually every rubric dimension at or near the ceiling. The double-weighted dimensions (R3, R5) are both 5: rule-outs are specific, terminal, and framed so the user cannot waste time on those funders again; the set is consistent with what a senior UK fundraising consultant would recommend, including the CIC structural filter, Brighton & Hove geographic nuance, and the earned-income prompt. The only meaningful gaps are a slightly soft challenge posture (R6) and some structural verbosity that slightly dilutes the 'relief' feel (R7). No errors of fact or judgment were detected. A very strong overall performance.

A strong output that earns its scores on the double-weighted dimensions (R1, R2). The binding constraint is named precisely and immediately; the sequencing is genuinely argued with the between-rounds Docklands fixture correctly framed as 'prepare for September' rather than open-now. The arithmetic is put to work throughout. The main weakness is R3: the Ellerdale rule-out rests on an absence of data in the feed (£0–£0 amount) rather than a positive disqualifying fact from the pack, and a senior consultant would flag that a likely_eligible verdict deserves more than a 'can't see the quantum' dismissal — either a 'check required' action or a stronger evidenced rule-out. R4 is clean but one sourcing gap (the community learning fund deadline) prevents a 5. R6 is good but misses the most important challenge: whether the £750k target itself remains viable given the arithmetic. Overall this is a well-disciplined, consultant-grade output.

A high-quality output that handles all three double-weighted dimensions (R3, R7, R5) well. Rule-outs are specific and closed off properly; the load is proportionate to a £15k goal; the consultant-level instincts (credibility ladder, restricted-income flag, non-cash exclusion of pool-cre-4) are sound. The two small gaps are: (1) the six-week micro-grant decision window is not explicitly named as a pacing anchor (case guidance calls this out); (2) the all-restricted-income challenge, while present, is in a secondary section rather than foregrounded. Neither is a serious failure. Overall a strong 4+ output, just below a clean 5 on R5 and R7.

A strong output that genuinely earns its scores. R4 (fact/judgment separation) is exemplary and deserves the 5. R1 (constraint-first) is excellent. R3 (rule-out quality) is the weakest dimension relative to the case guidance: the secured loan is ruled out with the right reasons but the catalogue field citation (siSecurityRequired) is absent, and the case guidance explicitly flags this as the differentiating detail. R5 and R6 share a common gap: the 25% investment mix target is never challenged as itself potentially unrealistic for a pre-revenue asset-locked org — a genuinely senior consultant would surface that. R2 is solid but the mix-target ordering rationale is slightly mechanical. Overall this is a well-structured, honest, actionable output that treats stage-awareness as the organising fact — the core test for this case.

A strong output. The double-weighted dimensions (R1, R7, R4) all score well: the constraint-first opening is genuinely excellent and precisely grounded; fact/judgment separation is exemplary throughout; and the recommendation count is disciplined at four total actions. R2 sequencing is well-argued with explicit deadline-awareness. R3 rule-outs are specific and dispositive. The only areas holding it back from a clean sweep are: R6 (questions are adequate but the agent doesn't actively push back on any user assumption or invite challenge on a specific judgment), and a mild R5/R7 tension around whether pool-cre-2 deserves inclusion given a part-time fundraiser's capacity — the agent flags its modesty but still recommends applying, which a very senior consultant might question. No serious errors; no hallucinated facts; no judgment smuggled as fact.

rubric.note: The output fails at its most critical moment: the user asked specifically about the Stronger Women fund, the pack makes clear the org cannot clear the 80% women-and-girls threshold, and the case guidance is explicit that a 5 says no clearly, cites the threshold verbatim, and names the cost to the user. The agent instead recommends applying with caveats and never mentions the 80% line. On the two double-weighted dimensions (R3, R6) this is a 2 on both — not because the output is careless, but because it fails precisely where it needed to succeed. R5 follows the same failure. The structural quality (fact/judgment separation, constraint-led narrative, sourcing discipline) is genuinely good and would score well in a less critical scenario, but the core professional judgment is wrong in a way that could cause real harm to a user who trusts the tool.

rubric.note: A strong output that earns high marks on constraint-first framing, fact/judgment discipline, and load-reduction. The critical failure is R3: the investigate recommendation names 'Sport England Unites Crowd' and 'Greater Manchester Combined Authority sport and community programmes' as specific prospecting targets — exactly the fabricated or unverified local specifics the case guidance flags as must_not_mention territory. The pack supports no such named schemes, and the agent should have pointed at source types (local community foundation, active partnership) without asserting scheme names. This is the single most important failure given the double-weighting of R3 and R5. All other dimensions are above average to excellent. If the named-scheme references were replaced with source-type pointers only, this would be a near-exemplary output.

A strong output that correctly identifies the binding constraint, executes the England-only trap detection well, and maintains impeccable fact/judgment separation. The misclassification flag on syn-wales-culture is genuinely consultant-grade. The main gap — material for the double-weighted R5/R3 case — is the failure to explicitly scope Welsh-language-specific funding routes as a distinct category from general Welsh sources, and to direct the user to Welsh-language sector sources as a named gap ('coverage here is partial; cross-check Welsh-language sector sources'). The case guidance treats this as a 5-vs-2 differentiator and the agent only partially delivers it. No England-only funder leaks into the final recommendation set, which is correctly managed.

rubric.note: A strong output. The case's planted temptation (Bright Minds as strongest thematic fit) is correctly resisted, with the right nuance that the exclusion is time-limited to 2028 rather than permanent. The Westbrook relationship reframe is executed correctly — 'continuation rather than a cold application' and 'pre-submission conversation' for stewardship. Both org_facts are restated plainly in learned[]. Fact/judgment separation is the standout dimension — genuinely exemplary, every claim sourced and every judgment flagged as editorial. The main gaps preventing higher scores across R5–R7 are: the contract/corporate 'rebalance' recommendation lacks an actionable next step; the rule-out funder names (Learning Futures Trust, Regional CF) appear to be synthetic names not verifiable from the briefing pack, introducing a small fabrication risk in R3; and the output could push the user slightly harder on the alarming pipeline-empty situation in R6.

This is a high-quality output. The double-weighted dimensions (R3 and R4) are both exemplary: the gambling exclusion is applied at exactly the right scope (constraint respected, lottery carve-out preserved), and fact/judgment separation is rigorous and consistent throughout. R1 is genuinely constraint-first. The main headroom for improvement is in R5 (the evidence-pack recommendation is generically safe rather than strategically sharp) and R6 (the output stops just short of a direct challenge on target achievability given zero pipeline and a thin market). R7 is good but not quite 'relief' — four recommendations plus flags plus questions is a lot to absorb in one sitting, and the evidence-base action could have been cut or merged without loss.

A technically disciplined response that handles the dual ask (capacity grant + in-kind) correctly and maintains rigorous fact/judgment separation throughout. The main failure is the opening paragraph: the user explicitly flagged 'different question' and the agent's first sentence still leads with the £1.5m gap arithmetic — the case guidance calls this 'caging' and explicitly forbids it. The in-kind recommendation is honest about undisclosed value and rolling access but omits the 4-8 week matching timeline that would help the user calibrate. Rule-outs is empty for the right reason (none in annex) but the absence isn't explained constructively. The kind-challenge questions are genuinely good. On the double-weighted dimensions: R5 is a solid 4 (sector-literate, correct candidates, one gap on matching timeline); R7 is a 4 (concise and action-oriented, slightly undermined by the unnecessary gap-arithmetic opener). No dimension is catastrophically wrong; the ceiling is the caging failure in R1 and the thin rule-out explanation in R3.

rubric.note: A strong output. The double-weighted dimensions (R7, R2, R1) all score 4 or 5, which is the right result for a case where the test is 'what do you do with abundance.' The agent correctly identifies concentration risk as the binding constraint, sequences by deadline window and capacity logic, accounts for truncation explicitly in the selection_summary flag, and keeps the shortlist to four items (three apply + one investigate). The main friction points are: (1) the fourth 'investigate' recommendation partially duplicates the flags section, adding load without adding decision value; (2) there is no explicit invitation to challenge the agent's own prioritisation — the kind challenge operates only at the application level, not at the recommendation-set level; (3) the rule-out section is technically correct but not stress-tested beyond the single eligible-but-timed-out entry, which is low-difficulty given the pool structure. The output would serve a senior UK fundraising director well as a first-pass brief.

rubric.note: Strong structural output that leads correctly with the binding constraint, sequences with genuine arguments, and separates facts from judgments in its architecture. The critical failure is R4 (double-weighted): the agent invents grant ranges of '£10,000–£30,000' for Harvest Trust and '£15,000–£25,000' for Larder Network, citing catalogue fields — amounts the briefing pack does not disclose. Per case guidance, inventing any number is a gate-level failure. The narrative compounds this by relying on 'maximum disclosed amounts' as if these figures were real. R3 also underperforms: with an empty rule-out annex the agent had an opportunity to explain the absence substantively but instead left the field empty with only a one-line flag note. The output would be genuinely excellent with those two issues corrected.

A strong, well-structured output that gets the most important things right: constraint-first narrative using pack arithmetic, deadline-driven sequencing with explicit rationale, a clean rule-out, and a manageable set of recommendations. The primary failures are (a) not marking the conversion-rate inference as judgment — the exact error the guidance flags — and (b) asking the wrong first question (should be: when does the £120k national funder bid decision come?). R2 and R1 are near-misses for 5. R4 is the weakest dimension and is the one double-weighted by the case guidance, which keeps the overall ceiling lower than the structural quality might otherwise suggest.

A strong output overall. The three double-weighted dimensions (R3, R5, R7) are all handled well: the oversized fund is ruled out with the specific figure (£500k–£5m vs £120k goal), the set and its priorities pass the consultant test without anything naive, and the load is reasonably reduced. The slight drag on R7 is structural — the JSON verbosity means a non-specialist reader must work harder than necessary to extract the action list, and the pacing flag deserves more prominence. R6 is good but not quite a 5 because the agent doesn't explicitly invite the client to challenge whether the £120k goal is achievable at all given the arithmetic — it observes the gap but doesn't push back on the goal itself.
